overview: The atlas paints a White Sheep realm in 1492 to 1530, although its greatest ruler was dead and the empire broke apart before the layer ended. Aq Qoyunlu, or White Sheep, was a Bayandur-led Turkmen confederation whose leaders linked seasonal pasture networks, old cities, tribal armies and Persian administration. Uzun Hasan defeated rivals and ruled from Tabriz; his son Yaqub supported scholars and artists. Then princes and commanders fought for control. Shah Ismail defeated major claimants in 1501 and took remaining lands by 1508, while smaller branches lasted longer. This card treats the polygon as a map layer, not a perfect border. It follows councils, taxes, royal women, camp work, meals, books, carpets, hospitals, baths and one elusive toilet, and shows how people and artistic skills continued under Safavid and Ottoman rule.

periods.title: A Bayandur confederation takes root
periods.summary: White Sheep Turkmen leaders built a principality around Diyarbakir. Qara Osman aided Timur, gained Amid and strengthened a coalition that still depended on tribal allies and local settled communities.

periods.title: A succession struggle after Qara Osman
periods.summary: Qara Osman's death opened years of rivalry among relatives and tribal factions. Uzun Hasan eventually took Amid in 1452, but his rise came through negotiation and fighting inside a loose confederation.

periods.title: Uzun Hasan reunites the western base
periods.summary: From Amid, Uzun Hasan outmaneuvered family rivals, cultivated alliances and expanded across eastern Anatolia. His household and Bayandur emblem became centers for a much larger political project.

periods.title: Empire, Tabriz and the Ottoman check
periods.summary: Victories over Jahanshah and the Timurid Abu Said brought Iran and Iraq under Uzun Hasan, who ruled from Tabriz. Ottoman firearms helped stop his westward challenge at Otlukbeli in 1473.

periods.title: Yaqub's court holds the realm together
periods.summary: After a brief contest, Yaqub presided over relative calm. His court supported scholars and manuscripts, but disputes over land, taxation and powerful confederate families remained beneath the surface.

periods.title: Child princes and rival coalitions
periods.summary: Yaqub's death was followed by rapid successions and competing claimants. Rostam briefly used Safavid followers against a rival, while faction leaders turned young princes into banners for their own coalitions.

periods.title: Safavid conquest, remnants and an atlas afterimage
periods.summary: Ismail defeated Alvand in 1501 and took Aq Qoyunlu lands through 1508. Small dynastic remnants survived longer, yet the atlas keeps one giant state painted until its 1530 Ottoman-Safavid handoff.

items.text: The repository's exact id is emirate-of-the-white-sheep-turks. Its display name is “Emirate of the White Sheep Turks,” its only alias is the very broad word “Turks,” and its circa dates are 1492 to 1530. Aq Qoyunlu is the linked historical identity; the alias must not swallow other Turkic peoples.

No exact target appears in the 1400 layer. A broad timurid-empire feature covers most later test points, but that is an atlas backdrop rather than a trustworthy claim that Timurids governed every town and pasture. Historically, the White Sheep confederation was already active around Diyarbakir before this missing snapshot.

At 1492 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 225 positions. Its bounding box runs from about 37.95° to 60.48° east and 25.30° to 43.86° north. Tests place Diyarbakir, Tabriz, Baghdad, Isfahan, Shiraz and Kerman inside, but Erzincan, Aleppo, Trebizond and Herat outside.

The 1500 feature again has one part, one ring and 225 positions, with the same tested inclusions and exclusions as 1492. Only tiny coordinate-transform differences change its hash. That near-static paint is historically misleading: rival White Sheep princes were dividing authority while a new Safavid coalition gathered strength.

At 1530 the id disappears. The atlas gives most western and northern tests to ottoman-empire and Iranian tests to safavid-empire, yet it even puts tested Tabriz on the Ottoman side. This is a rough editorial handoff, useful for navigation but much too blunt to settle an exact frontier or conquest date.

sections.title: A name, a confederation and an older story

items.text: Aq Qoyunlu means “White Sheep,” but historians do not know exactly why the confederation used that name. Ideas about sheep colors or animal emblems remain hypotheses. The safe fact is political: Bayandur leaders headed a changing alliance of Turkmen groups, not a modern nation with fixed membership and borders.

In the mid-fourteenth century, associated groups moved seasonally between summer pastures in Armenia east of Bayburt and winter country around Kigi, Palu and Ergani near Diyarbakir. That circuit joined herds, camps and towns. It was planned mobility through known landscapes, not people drifting without routes or destinations.

Qara Osman helped Timur around 1399 to 1400, received rank and control around Amid, and made that city the dynasty's main center for roughly seventy years. Diyarbakir's walls enclosed older communities and institutions, so building a Turkmen principality meant governing an inhabited region rather than founding a capital on empty ground.

The ruling label did not describe everyone inside it. Armenian Christians, Kurdish and Arab communities, townspeople and villagers lived beside Turkmen pastoral and military groups. Evidence from Armenia especially warns against turning the dynasty's language or religion into a population census: subjects could keep distinct churches, occupations and local ties.

Bayandur descent helped rulers explain why their house should lead, and a Bayandur tamga, a compact clan emblem, appeared on coins, documents, inscriptions and banners under Uzun Hasan. Imagine a political logo small enough for silver yet bold enough for a flag; it signaled dynasty, not a complete list of everybody's identity.

sections.title: How Uzun Hasan made an empire

items.text: Uzun Hasan took Amid in 1452 and gradually defeated relatives and rivals. His greatest leap came in 1467 to 69, when victories over the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Jahanshah and the Timurid Abu Said opened Azerbaijan, Iran and Iraq. Government shifted toward Tabriz, while Diyarbakir remained an important western base.

Baghdad came under Uzun Hasan and later remained connected to Yaqub and Sultan Murad. Holding such a famous city expanded revenues and prestige, but distance mattered: a confederation stretching from Anatolia into Iraq and Iran depended on governors, tribal commanders, roads and bargains that a colored polygon cannot show.

Isfahan entered Uzun Hasan's realm after 1470, and its urban life began to revive. That is a better achievement than simply counting conquered square miles: towns could reconnect to court demand, trade and administration. Recovery was uneven, however, and one city's improvement cannot be projected across every place inside the huge atlas shape.

Uzun Hasan exchanged envoys with Venice while searching for allies against the Ottomans. Ambrogio Contarini reached his court in 1474 after a difficult journey and later wrote a valuable report. As a diplomat seeking policy and access, he saw elite spaces especially clearly; he was not conducting a household survey.

On 11 August 1473, Ottoman cannon and handguns helped defeat Uzun Hasan at Otlukbeli. Venetian firearms promised to his side never arrived in time. He lost little core territory immediately, but the defeat checked his westward plans, a sharp reminder that diplomacy, supply routes and technology could matter as much as courage.

sections.title: Councils, officials, taxes and tiny silver

items.text: The sultan did not command a modern machine. A council of amirs and tribal chiefs could constrain major decisions, because those leaders supplied followers and military strength. Personal guards helped rulers, but coalition politics remained essential. “Confederation” therefore describes a working power relationship, not merely a loose nickname.

Turkmen commanders stood near the military top, while settled specialists kept farms, workshops, trade and offices working. Regional economic history distinguishes pastoral production, village agriculture and urban commerce, but they constantly exchanged animals, grain, labor and manufactured goods. Social rank and livelihood crossed the simple nomad-versus-city line.

Uzun Hasan's qanun regulated taxes and trade charges, and later governments remembered parts of it. Rates still differed by district, crop and older custom, so “law code” should not suggest one neat modern tax form. For villagers and merchants, the practical achievement was an attempt to limit or standardize what collectors demanded.

Land and revenue assignments helped reward commanders, yet they also made central control difficult when powerful holders resisted change. Scholars debate Aq Qoyunlu reform efforts and their reach. The honest version for young readers is that changing a rule on paper did not instantly change who controlled fields, taxes or armed followers.

A surviving silver quarter tanka of Yaqub from Sultaniyah is only 11 millimetres wide and weighs 1.15 grams, smaller than many shirt buttons. Coins paid, measured and advertised authority at once. This undated piece proves minting under his name, but one tiny object cannot tell us what every market customer carried.

sections.title: The atlas begins during the breakup

items.text: Yaqub died on 24 December 1490; sources disagree over plague or poison. Afterward, powerful factions backed young princes, and short reigns followed. This means the atlas's first painted year, 1492, does not show the confident empire of Uzun Hasan. It opens inside a succession crisis already two years old.

Rostam became a leading claimant around the atlas start. In 1493 he released the imprisoned Safavid brothers and used their followers against a rival, then turned against them when their strength looked dangerous. The episode shows how rapidly allies became threats and why a prince's name alone could not stabilize the confederation.

By 1500 rival White Sheep rulers and regional power holders competed while the atlas still displayed one unchanged giant polygon. Ismail emerged from Gilan, gathered Qizilbash supporters and advanced toward Azerbaijan. The visual continuity is therefore the opposite of political continuity: steady paint covers a fast-moving struggle.

Ismail defeated Alvand near Sharur and entered Tabriz in 1501. He took Fars and central Iran by 1503 to 04, Diyarbakir by about 1505 to 07, and Baghdad in 1508. Those stages dismantled the major Aq Qoyunlu realms decades before the atlas removes their single state in 1530.

The 1508 capture of Iraq marks the final major Safavid victory over Aq Qoyunlu power. Some small family branches and claimants survived beyond the central empire, but they did not continuously rule from Diyarbakir to Shiraz. The card keeps 1530 only as map coverage and explains the earlier political ending.

sections.title: Families, women and very unequal lives

items.text: Saray Khatun, Uzun Hasan's mother, negotiated among rulers and traveled on diplomatic missions, including talks with Ottoman leaders. Her record proves that one royal woman could exercise serious political skill. It does not prove equal power for ordinary women, whose work and choices appear far less often in surviving chronicles.

Despina Khatun was a Christian Greek princess from Trebizond who married Uzun Hasan in a 1458 alliance and retained her faith. She participated in court politics and diplomacy. Her life makes the ruling family visibly cross-cultural, although a dynastic marriage was also a strategy between states, not a fairy-tale romance.

Family ties could redraw politics. Despina's daughter married the Safavid leader Haydar and became mother of Ismail, so the young conqueror who defeated Aq Qoyunlu rulers was also Uzun Hasan's grandson. Kinship did not prevent war; it supplied claims, allies, hostages and rival branches for ambitious leaders to use.

A contemporary history remembered the teenage Uzun Hasan with one blue-cloth outfit, a felt cloak and one horse; fodder could be so scarce that he often walked. The picture is unusually human and perhaps crafted to celebrate later success. Even future emperors could face sore feet, but this is one prince's story.

Most family life remains quieter than royal genealogy. Pastoral households, farming villages, craft neighborhoods, servants and enslaved people had different risks and resources. Children often learned through work beside relatives, an inference from those economies rather than a preserved Aq Qoyunlu timetable. No source checked supplies an average family size.

sections.title: Camp roads, farms, bazaars and dinner

items.text: Contarini watched an Aq Qoyunlu camp move toward better pasture and water. He said women arrived first, put up the tents and prepared for their husbands. This is vivid evidence of women's skilled camp labor in a particular elite traveling community; it is not a rulebook for every family or every move.

At court, Contarini saw hundreds sit on the ground for meals served in copper vessels, with rice or grain and a little meat. Court provisioning could feed a crowd, but this was not an ordinary supper menu. Wealth, season, region and access to herds or farms changed what people ate.

Rural producers grew crops and cared for animals while towns concentrated workshops, markets and administration. These were linked livelihoods: city diners needed grain and meat, herders needed metalwork and cloth, and rulers needed taxes from both. The precise mix varied from Diyarbakir's countryside to Iranian cities and dry uplands.

Barbaro described about one hundred pavilions at a festival near Tabriz and inspected forty of the finest. Their rooms had colored coverings and carpets he judged finer than famous work from Cairo or Bursa. It is spectacular elite display, not evidence that every child slept on a museum-quality rug.

Barbaro's report records court feasts, dancing, wrestling and unusual animals as well as routes, goods and settlements. A wrestling bout or exotic beast may have been the day's best entertainment, but his eye followed diplomatic novelty. Ordinary games, jokes and work breaks are much less visible than royal spectacle.

Uzun Hasan held gatherings with scholars on Friday nights. A reading of al-Bukhari's hadith collection was reportedly explained or translated into Turkish for him, showing learned Arabic material moving into a court's spoken language. This was advanced royal study, not proof that every child attended school or read Arabic.

The astronomer and mathematician Ali Qushji received a warm welcome and gifts from Uzun Hasan, who then sent him onward as an envoy to the Ottoman court. A scholar could therefore carry mathematics, astronomy and diplomacy along the same roads. Patronage helped knowledge travel, although access remained highly unequal.

At Yaqub's court, Shams al-Din Muhammad al-Kubanani composed a commentary connected with Euclid. A catalogue records a scholarly eulogy dated at Tabriz on 7 January 1483, while the manuscript itself remained unfinished. Geometry at court was real; a dated learned book still does not reveal ordinary literacy rates.

A royal-library copy of Hidayat's poetry was written in southern Turkmen Turkish in Arabic script and marked for Sultan Khalil, whose sudden death in 1478 may explain why the manuscript was unfinished. Books could be beautiful political objects as well as texts, and incompleteness can itself preserve a historical moment.

The manuscript opens with the exact short fragment “ای جان و کونکل.” A cautious editorial transliteration is “Ey cān u göñül,” literally “O soul and heart!” It is southern Turkmen Turkish in Arabic script from a royal poetry book, not everyday dialogue; the transliteration and translation are labels, not a facsimile.

sections.title: Pictures and buildings that outlived rulers

items.text: The Khavarnama made in Shiraz around 1476 to 86 once filled roughly 685 folios with the legendary adventures of Ali. Its painters used ink, opaque watercolor, silver and gold for battles involving kings, demons and dragons. A dragon is excellent page-turning evidence, though the tale is literature, not a news report.

A Tabriz frontispiece dedicated to Sultan Khalil combined ink, gold and opaque watercolor with Timurid and Turkmen artistic traditions. Khalil ruled for only six months in 1478, yet the page survived far longer than his reign. Objects can preserve ambition even when politics changes before the paint has faded.

A fifteenth-century Shiraz page from Nizami's Khamsa uses ink, watercolor, silver and gold, with a painting style linked to Sultan Khalil's Aq Qoyunlu period. Manuscript workshops did not start over whenever a ruler changed: artists reused designs, skills and stories while patrons and political labels shifted.

Tabriz's Blue Mosque complex was completed in 1465 under the rival Qara Qoyunlu, before Uzun Hasan conquered the city. Its garden, qanat and possible school and bath became part of the inherited capital. Aq Qoyunlu rulers used an existing urban landscape; they did not build every impressive monument inside their territory.

Diyarbakir's Nebi Mosque is commonly linked to the fifteenth-century Aq Qoyunlu period, but its minaret inscription dates that component to 1530. The date matches the atlas endpoint and could fool a quick reader. It records a later building phase, not proof that a White Sheep emperor still ruled the city.

sections.title: Hospitals, water, baths, and the missing toilet

items.text: At Mardin, Barbaro stayed in a charitable hospital or hospice founded by Jahangir, Uzun Hasan's brother. It fed visitors and gave high-status guests carpeted accommodation. Medieval “hospital” could combine lodging, food and care, so this evidence should not be translated automatically into a modern clinic with identical wards and treatments.

Yaqub's Hasht Behesht complex in Tabriz included a bimaristan, a care institution often translated as hospital. A later Venetian account claimed room for more than a thousand poor patients or residents. That impressive number is a retrospective report, not an audited bed count, but it supports organized charitable care.

Bathhouses in Iranian cities drew water through wells or conduits and often placed hot rooms partly underground. A traveler said Tabriz palaces had baths, revealing elite water infrastructure rather than universal indoor plumbing. Bathing served cleanliness and sociability, but surviving descriptions do not measure how often poorer residents could enter.

Excavations in Diyarbakir's citadel found Roman clean- and waste-water channels and an Artuqid palace bath and heating system. Those older layers show long engineering traditions, but they are not securely identified Aq Qoyunlu toilets. No source checked documents a dynasty-wide sewer network or a specific White Sheep household latrine.

A visitor described Tabriz garden channels and bronze dragon spouts pouring water near swans. The scene helps explain why water displays impressed travelers after the dynasty fell, while proving nothing about toilet sanitation. Dragons got plumbing; historians are still looking for the securely dated Aq Qoyunlu privy.

ending.text: The 1530 endpoint is an atlas handoff, not the dynasty's political death. Safavid victories dismantled its main Iranian and Iraqi realms by 1508, while smaller branches and claimants lasted longer. The layer then divides tested lands mainly between Ottoman and Safavid features. Political rule changed, while artists in Safavid Tabriz combined inherited Aq Qoyunlu and Timurid painting traditions.
